body:
Thanks for the unusually thorough report — the `_features` patch and the before/after measurements made this quick to confirm.

## Your result is right; the Tahoe claim isn't

The cap is still on by default in current WebKit trunk. From `Source/WTF/Scripts/Preferences/UnifiedWebPreferences.yaml`:

```yaml
PreferPageRenderingUpdatesNear60FPSEnabled:
  type: bool
  status: stable
  defaultValue:
    WebKit:
      "PLATFORM(VISION)": false
      default: true          # macOS included, no SDK or OS version gate
```

visionOS is the only port that opts out, and there is no `linkedOnOrAfter`/SDK check anywhere near it — so building against the 26.5 SDK cannot change it. What it does is in `platform/graphics/AnimationFrameRate.cpp`, via `Page::preferredRenderingUpdateFramesPerSecond`:

```cpp
FramesPerSecond framesPerSecondNearestFullSpeed(FramesPerSecond nominal) {
    if (nominal <= 60) return nominal;
    float ratio = nominal / 60;
    ...  // 120 → 120/2 = 60,  165 → 165/3 = 55
}
```

Your 120 → 60 is that function exactly. So the compatibility table in `tauri-plugin-macos-fps` is simply wrong for macOS 26 — which your own Safari 26 observation already shows, since Safari defaults to 60 there too. Nothing about how Wails creates the `WKWebView` is involved, and `suppressesIncrementalRendering` was never going to matter.

## There is no public API, and I looked hard

- **`WKPreferences`** ships ten public properties; none concern frame rate. Same for `WKWebViewConfiguration` and `WKWebpagePreferences`.
- **NSUserDefaults.** `WebPreferencesCocoa.mm` does read preferences from user defaults, but every getter begins `if (!m_identifier) return false;`, and a `WKPreferences` built with the public `init` has no identifier. The second path, for `defaultsOverridable` preferences, works without one — but nothing in the YAML opts into it. So `defaults write` can't reach it either.
- **Info.plist / entitlements.** No such gate exists in the source. (`CADisableMinimumFrameDurationOnPhone` is public but iOS-only, and only affects Core Animation.)
- **The near miss:** `Page::preferredRenderingUpdateFramesPerSecond` takes the *max* of the capped rate and any explicitly requested animation rate, and WebKit already implements `animation.frameRate = "highest"` on `WebAnimation`. That would fix this from JavaScript with no native code at all — except it's gated behind `WebAnimationsCustomFrameRateEnabled`, which is `status: testable` and defaults to `false` on every port. Enabling it needs the same private API. Worth lobbying WebKit for; it's the only route that ends in a supported API.

So you were right not to suggest we just ship the `_features` workaround by default.

## What we're doing instead: opt-in, and off in App Store builds

[#6060](https://github.com/wailsapp/wails/pull/6060) moves every private macOS API Wails uses into one guarded file, and adds a per-window option:

```go
app.Window.NewWithOptions(application.WebviewWindowOptions{
    Mac: application.MacWindow{
        WebviewPreferences: application.MacWebviewPreferences{
            PreferPageRenderingUpdatesNear60FPS: application.Disabled,
        },
    },
})
```

It mirrors the WebKit flag name rather than inventing one, so it's obvious what it maps to. It is applied to the `WKPreferences` **before** the `WKWebView` is created — worth noting, because `-[WKWebView configuration]` returns a copy, so a post-init change isn't guaranteed to reach the web process even though it appeared to work in your test.

Because it's a private API, it's opt-in, and building with `-tags appstore` turns it (and every other private call Wails makes) into a public equivalent or a no-op. Your app decides whether to accept the risk, rather than Wails deciding for everyone. The option also degrades to a logged no-op if a future WebKit drops the flag, instead of crashing.

## Could you test it?

The branch is `claude/wails-120fps-public-apis-h3bnby`. The Objective-C was written and reviewed on Linux and **has not been compiled on a Mac yet**, so a second pair of eyes on real hardware would genuinely help before this leaves draft. In your app:

```
go mod edit -replace github.com/wailsapp/wails/v3=github.com/wailsapp/wails/v3@claude/wails-120fps-public-apis-h3bnby
go mod tidy
```

Three things worth checking, if you have the time:

1. Your `requestAnimationFrame` counter with the option set to `application.Disabled` — does it reach ~120 the way your manual patch did?
2. A default build with the option **unset** — is everything unchanged? The refactor touched transparent, translucent, Liquid Glass and notch windows, so any regression there is the thing most likely to bite.
3. A build with `-tags appstore` — it should compile, stay at 60fps, and contain none of the private selectors.

One caveat worth stating: higher frame rates cost more GPU time and battery, so this is a per-window opt-in rather than a new default.
